lens: Fact integrity: every checkable claim in the published essay (client/public/essays/did-god-command-genocide.json, byte-identical to the draft docs/work/essays/did-god-command-genocide.md) traced to its ledger line and, where risky, rechecked against primary texts (TCP Underhill A14203 and Mason N03314, WDB Tertullian and Augustine files, the ESV copy, the site's BSB chapter files) and 10 web searches this run.

findings.where: Section 'What These Chapters Have Been Used For', paragraph 3, first sentence: "Underhill was not the last American Christian to read Canaan onto the people whose land he wanted." Also paragraph 1 of the same section: "so that English soldiers could play Israel and the Pequots could play Canaan."
findings.problem: (c) Mismatch between ledger evidence and essay. The essay says Underhill read Canaan onto the Pequots and wanted their land. This run searched the full TCP transcription of Underhill's Newes from America (A14203): it never mentions Canaan, Joshua, Jericho, Amalek or the Amorites. At the point the essay quotes, his only named precedent is "Davids warre" (the Ammonite campaign, harrows and saws). The ledger itself notes this (Mystic section, 'Note for the editor'). The ledger's support for the sentence (section 'What these chapters have been used for') is John Mason, not Underhill: Mason's preface, signed "Farewell John Mason," says "the LORD was as it were pleased to say unto us, The Land of Canaan will I give unto thee" (TCP N03314, reread this run). No seen source shows that Underhill personally wanted Pequot land.
findings.fix: Replace "Underhill was not the last American Christian to read Canaan onto the people whose land he wanted." with "The English at Mystic were not the last American Christians to read Canaan onto the people whose land they wanted." If the writer wants Mason named, use instead: "Underhill's fellow captain, John Mason, opened his own history of the war by saying the Lord had as it were told the English, "The Land of Canaan will I give unto thee." They were not the last American Christians to read Canaan onto the people whose land they wanted." (Mason's words are verbatim from TCP N03314; add a ledger line for the quotation.) In paragraph 1, replace "so that English soldiers could play Israel and the Pequots could play Canaan." with "so that English soldiers could play Israel and the Pequots could play Israel's enemies." Then update the ledger's 'Withheld links' restore instruction so it anchors on the new sentence instead of the old one.

findings.where: Section 'How Ancient War Reports Talk', paragraph 4: "Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan built a whole book on that reading, under nearly the same title as this essay."
findings.problem: (f) Overclaim about two living authors. The ledger verified only that chapters 6 to 8 of Did God Really Command Genocide? make the hyperbole case. Reviews seen this run show the book does more than that. An Academia.edu review says its Part 3 explores divine command theory and the killing of innocents. Pursuing Veritas says that part argues it is possible and morally permissible to affirm that God can, in certain instances, command the killing of innocents. So the book is not built wholly on the hyperbole reading.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan made that reading central to a book under nearly the same title as this essay." The next sentence ("What God required, they argue, ...") stays as it is.

findings.where: Section 'What the Text Says the War Was For', paragraph 6: "Leviticus had warned Israel that the land would vomit them out as well (Leviticus 18:28), and in the end Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and carried its people into exile."
findings.problem: (g) Restoration. Ledger Corrections item 9 records the original wording "in 586 BC Babylon destroyed Jerusalem". It was generalized because the year could not be checked. A search this run saw the ESV Global Study Bible map page on esv.org ("in 586 Nebuchadnezzar completely destroyed the walls of Jerusalem and the temple"). Wikipedia's 'Siege of Jerusalem (587 BC)' gives 587, and one summary said most encyclopedias give 587. So the date is confirmed only as 587 or 586. The bare "in 586 BC" should not come back. A hedged form matching the essay's own "Around 1208 BC" and "Around 840 BC" is supported.
findings.fix: Replace "and in the end Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and carried its people into exile." with "and in the end, around 586 BC, Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and carried its people into exile." Update ledger item 9 and the Babylon line to cite the esv.org Global Study Bible map and the 587/586 split.

findings.where: Section 'Jesus and the Canaanite Woman', paragraph 2: "Mark calls her a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth. Matthew calls her "a Canaanite woman," and she is the only person ..."
findings.problem: (e) Mark 7:26 ESV reads "Now the woman was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth." The essay uses those exact ESV words without quotation marks and without a reference, while the parallel Matthew phrase in the next sentence is quoted. That phrase's reference (Matthew 15:22) is two sentences back. The ledger accepts the Mark wording as unquoted use.
findings.fix: Mark calls her "a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth" (Mark 7:26). Matthew calls her "a Canaanite woman" (Matthew 15:22), and she is the only person in the New Testament given that name.

findings.where: Section 'What the Commands Say', last paragraph: "I can't read "child and infant" as a puzzle in biblical interpretation"
findings.problem: (e) A quoted ESV phrase with no reference beside it. The reference (1 Samuel 15:3) is two paragraphs earlier. BRIEF asks for the reference beside each Scripture quotation.
findings.fix: I can't read "child and infant" (1 Samuel 15:3) as a puzzle in biblical interpretation, and I don't think any Christian should try.

findings.where: Section 'What the Text Says the War Was For', last paragraph: ""They deserved it" is what armies always say about the towns they burn. Underhill said it about the Pequots." Also section 'What These Chapters Have Been Used For', paragraph 3: "the move Underhill made, from "God judged them" to "God is with us against them,""
findings.problem: (d) Quotation marks set beside Underhill's name around words he never wrote. TCP Underhill has neither "They deserved it" nor "God judged them" nor "God is with us against them". What he wrote is that "a people is growne to such a height of bloud, and sinne against God and man". The sense is supported, but a reader checking Newes from America will not find these words. BRIEF: quotation marks hold only verbatim words.
findings.fix: Change "Underhill said it about the Pequots." to "Underhill said as much about the Pequots." Change the second passage to: "But the move Underhill made, from God judged them to God is with us against them, comes easily to the human heart", with the two phrases in italics (*God judged them*, *God is with us against them*) and no quotation marks.

findings.where: Ledger docs/work/essays/ledgers/did-god-command-genocide.md, section 'The three readings today', hyperbole line ("two details open") and the line "The essay leaves the choice among the three readings open ... Still open"
findings.problem: (b) Two ledger lines are still marked open while the essay states their content. (1) The essay says hyperbole readers point to "Rahab, and the stones of Merneptah and Mesha", and the ledger marks Rahab and Merneptah open. This run's searches closed both, at secondhand. A toughquestionsanswered.org summary of Copan and Flannagan presents Rahab as a Canaanite spared for her faith (Hebrews 11:31). A search summary of commentary on Copan says he cites Merneptah's line as ancient victory rhetoric, a "premature declaration", beside other boasts. (2) The ledger's 'Withheld links' note records that James decided on 2026-10-28 to publish with the three readings open, but the three-readings line still says "Needs James's position ... Still open."
findings.fix: No essay change. Update the hyperbole line to: "Verified in substance (final read, 2026-10-28): Rahab in Copan and Flannagan's case (toughquestionsanswered.org summary, citing Hebrews 11:31); Merneptah cited by Copan as victory rhetoric (search summary of commentary on his work)." Update the three-readings line to: "Settled: James decided on 2026-10-28 that the essay publishes with the three readings left open."

clean_checks: Draft docs/work/essays/did-god-command-genocide.md and published JSON body are identical (script diff).

All 37 Scripture quotations (including the three Closing Texts) match the ESV copy (lguenth/mdbible, 2011 text) by script after normalizing case and punctuation. Punctuation is ESV form: the exclamation points sit only inside Genesis 18:25 and Matthew 15:28.

Underhill quotations: "Sometimes the Scripture declareth women and children must perish with their parents" and "We had sufficient light from the word of God for our proceedings" both match TCP A14203 word for word (rechecked this run). The capital S and the split around the omitted "some-time the case alters" are signaled correctly.

Mystic facts: early morning ("breake of day"), May 26, 1637 (Mason/Prince citing Increase Mather), Connecticut and Massachusetts men, Mohegan and Narragansett allies, fire set by Mason and Underhill, people cut down outside, about 400 (Underhill) to 600-700 (Mason) dead. All rechecked in TCP texts. Newes from America, London, 1638, "the next year" verified.

Not restored: ledger item 1's original "most of them women, children and old men". A search this run saw World History Encyclopedia say the dead were mostly women, children and old men with the warriors away. But Mason (TCP N03314, read this run) says 150 men from the other fort had joined the village the night before and "perished with their Fellows". The proportion is disputed in the primary account, so the current "women and children among them" stays.

Lemkin (Polish Jewish lawyer, 1944), Convention adopted December 9, 1948, and the Article II wording "committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such" match the ledger's third-pass verification. "ethnical" is kept.

Merneptah (around 1208 BC, earliest known mention of Israel, "seed is no more" as paraphrase) and Mesha (around 840 BC, "perished forever", seven thousand at Nebo, the ban word) match ledger items 15 and 16 exactly, including the deliberate "seven thousand people at Nebo" and not "the seven thousand people of Nebo".
Younger (living) is described exactly as ledger item 17 corrected it: Egyptian, Hittite and Assyrian reports; sweeping claims in a stock, formulaic style. Fair to him.

Wolterstorff (living): the paraphrase that he found Joshua's totals were not meant as body counts is fair. This run's search saw the NDPR review of Divine Evil? call his hyperbole reading nuanced and defensible, and summaries of his Joshua/Judges contrast. His secondhand words are rightly not quoted.

Boyd (living): the description of The Crucifixion of the Warrior God, the Marcion objection and his defenders' reply is fair. This run's search saw a review saying "the charge of Marcionism" was leveled against the book, and Matt Lynch's review on re-reading texts to fit the cross.

Tertullian: "that Christ Jesus is the revealer of none other god but the Creator" matches WDB Against Marcion 1.19 verbatim (rechecked this run). Five books, Pontus, Antitheses, edited Luke and ten letters match the ledger.

Faustus: "destroyed thousands of men for a slight offense, or for nothing" and "threatened to come with a sword and spare nobody, righteous or wicked" match WDB Reply to Faustus 22.4 verbatim (rechecked).

Augustine: "not in cruelty, but in righteous retribution" and "Is it the death of some who will soon die in any case, that others may live in peaceful subjection?" match WDB 22.74 verbatim (rechecked). The framing "he asked what the evil in war really was" matches the preceding "What is the evil in war?"

Aquinas: thirteenth century; the paraphrase of I-II q.94 a.5 ad 2; and the quotation from "by the command of God" to "whatever" match ledger item 14 (the opening "Consequently," is dropped and the comma after God kept).
Origen: an unquoted paraphrase of Hom. Jos. 15.1, third century. It matches the ledger's third-pass sources and keeps no quotation marks.

Joshua/Jesus name: the Greek name in the LXX and the Gospels, Hebrews 4:8, and the KJV "Jesus" all match the ledger. Matthew 15:22 "Canaanite woman" as the only NT use of Chananaia matches the ledger's Greek-data check.
Creed paraphrase ("one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth") is unquoted and matches the 381 text in the ledger.
Biography: "I have five sons" is the only biography and is confirmed in NOTES. No title, years in ministry or book count.

Links: /writing/why-trust-the-bible ("Can You Trust the Bible?") and /writing/why-didnt-the-bible-ban-slavery both exist in client/public/essays. /help is allowed. The doctrine-of-discovery sentence is correctly withheld: there is no client/public/essays/doctrine-of-discovery.json and shelf.json still marks it pending.

Hedged general observations stay soft as the ledger asks: "often left out" (children's Bibles), "Many archaeologists", "Plenty of lifelong churchgoers". The defenders' summary ("any other reading lets the modern conscience overrule the text") is unquoted position-summary, as the ledger notes.
Joshua 15:63 "never driven out at all" is consistent with Judges 1:21 and 1 Kings 9:20-21. Judges 1:31 parenthesis (Sidon, not Tyre) matches correction item 4.
